levels.title: Heart
levels.about: Property parcels in a small city, one row per parcel.

tutorial.text: Click any hex in the painting. Each hex represents a feature, here a property parcel. Its row lights up in the attribute table under the painting, which lists every feature and its fields. Drag the bar above the table to make it bigger or smaller.
Click values next to the land_use field to list every value stored in it. Click a value to drop it into the query box. (Number fields show their range instead.)

Read the first request in the color key, Cream. Build land_use = 'residential' by clicking the field name, the = button and the value, or type it. Click Run. The parcels that match turn cyan: that’s your selection.
In step 2, choose Cream from the gem color menu and click Fill. When every gem for that request is in place, a ✓ appears next to it in the color key.
Now finish Ruby and Blush on your own. Check each field’s type first: floors is a NUMBER, so no quotes. zip looks like a number but is TEXT, so it needs quotes.

lesson: Every hex in the painting is a feature, and every feature has attributes: values stored in fields. Together they make the layer’s attribute table.
A query is a yes/no question asked of every feature. The ones that answer yes get selected.
To ask “is this field equal to this value?” write field = value. Numbers are written plain: acres = 12. Text goes inside single quotes: county = 'Kent'.

Look at each field’s type. Codes that look like numbers, like ZIP codes or phone numbers, are stored as TEXT because you never do math with them. A number field would also drop the leading zero in '02134'.

levels.title: Sunset

questions.question: A request asks for watersheds with a mean elevation of at least 850 m. Which condition matches?
hints: > leaves out a watershed at exactly 850 m.
= only picks watersheds at exactly 850 m.

questions.question: Which condition is written correctly?
questions.explain: The > comes before the =, and the number has no comma or quotes.
hints: SQL writes it >=, with the > first.
Leave the comma out of numbers.
pop is a number, so its values don’t get quotes.

questions.question: Which watersheds does mean_elev_m <> 400 select?
options: Every watershed except those at exactly 400 m
questions.explain: <> means “not equal to,” so it keeps everything above and below 400 m.
hints: <> isn’t “less than”: it means “not equal to.” What about watersheds above 400 m?
<> isn’t “greater than”: it means “not equal to.” What about watersheds below 400 m?

levels.about: Small watersheds across a mountain range, one polygon per watershed.
lesson: Not every question is “equals.” Numbers can be compared: > greater than, < less than, >= greater than or equal to, <= less than or equal to, and <> not equal to.
Watch the edges! pop > 5000 leaves out a town of exactly 5000. pop >= 5000 includes it. Requests say this in words: “more than,” “at least,” “or higher,” “or less.”
Leave commas out of numbers: write 1900, not 1,900.
This table has more fields than you need. Part of the job is figuring out which field answers each request.
Filling a hex replaces any color already there, like pressing a new gem on top. Work down the color key in order. Some colors are used for more than one request.

levels.title: Mushroom
levels.about: Field survey plots from a vegetation study, one row per plot.
lesson: Sometimes one condition isn’t enough. AND joins two conditions, and a feature is selected only if both are true.
land_use = 'farm' AND acres > 10 selects farms bigger than 10 acres. A small farm fails, and so does a big parking lot.
Each condition needs its own field name: write acres > 10 AND acres < 20, not acres > 10 AND < 20.
Requests rarely say “AND.” Listen for two facts about the same feature: “forest plots where invasive species were found.”

levels.title: Outlined cat
levels.dataset: Land ownership around Pine Ridge State Forest
levels.about: Land parcels in and around a state forest, one polygon per parcel.
lesson: Attribute queries ask about a feature’s values. Select by Location asks where a feature is in relation to other features.

Here the parcels are compared with the parcels you’ve already selected. Boundary touches picks parcels whose boundaries touch a selected parcel. Intersect picks parcels that share any area or boundary, so it also picks the selected parcels themselves.
Combine tools with the selection type: new replaces the selection, add to adds, remove from takes away, and select subset keeps only the parcels that pass the new test too.
Nothing in the attribute table says which parcels are next to the forest. Some questions can only be answered by location!
